en.title: Chemical Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What chemical engineering covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What chemical engineering is
sections.text:
Chemical engineering is the design and operation of processes that turn raw materials into useful products. The raw material may be crude oil, natural gas, mineral ore, air, water or a crop. The product may be fuel, fertiliser, plastic, cement, soap, food, a medicine or clean water. The engineer works out how to make the change safely, at large scale, and at a cost the market will pay.

The subject rests on a few big ideas. Material and energy balances say that nothing appears or disappears. Thermodynamics says which changes are possible and how much energy they need. Transport phenomena describe how fluids, heat and chemical species move. Reaction engineering says how fast a reaction goes and how large a reactor must be.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace design codes, standards or a registered engineer. Rules differ by country. In Nigeria, engineering practice is regulated under COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria. Check the current rules of your own country and your institution’s handbook.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
Length and award differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. A Nigerian BEng usually takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic students commonly take an ND (National Diploma), then supervised industrial work, then an HND (Higher National Diploma). In the UK a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four, with Scotland usually a year longer. Ghana, Kenya and other countries have their own patterns.

The early years are often shared with other engineers: mathematics, chemistry, physics, computing and drawing. Middle years carry the core: balances, thermodynamics, fluids, heat, mass transfer, reactions, control and safety. Final years add design, economics, environment and a plant design project. A master’s adds advanced analysis and a research dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
First comes the foundation: engineering mathematics, general chemistry, organic chemistry, physical chemistry, physics and computing. Engineering drawing and process diagrams belong here too, because you must read and draw a flowsheet before you can design one. An introduction to chemical engineering ties these together.

The core begins with material and energy balances, the language of the subject. Thermodynamics follows, then fluid mechanics, heat transfer and mass transfer. Distillation and the other separation topics apply mass transfer. Chemical reaction engineering applies thermodynamics and kinetics. Process control, particle technology, materials and corrosion, and process safety run alongside.

The later core is integrative: process design and economics, modelling and simulation, environmental engineering, biochemical engineering, and professional practice and ethics. The plant design project brings everything together. Master’s level covers advanced transport phenomena, advanced reaction engineering and catalysis, process systems engineering, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Work problems by hand, and often. Reading a solution is not the same as producing one. Draw the flowsheet or control volume first, then write the balance around it. Carry units on every line and ask whether the answer is sensible: is the pump power 3 kW or 300 kW?

Learn the small set of core equations well rather than many formulas vaguely. Practise the same problem in different unit systems. Use simulation software only after you can do the hand calculation, and check its output against a simple case.

Treat laboratory work and industrial training as evidence, not decoration. Record what you actually did, what you measured, and what went wrong.

keyPoints: Chemical engineering designs and runs processes that turn raw materials into useful products safely and profitably.
Material and energy balances, thermodynamics, transport phenomena and reaction engineering are the backbone of the subject.
Degree length and award differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
In Nigeria, engineering practice is regulated under COREN; other countries have their own bodies and rules.
Draw the flowsheet, carry units on every line, and check that answers are reasonable.
Understand the hand method before you trust software.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for chemical engineers
en.short: Calculus, linear algebra, ODEs, Laplace transforms, series and vector calculus for chemical engineering.

sections.heading: Calculus and balances
sections.text: Calculus studies change. The derivative dC/dt is the rate of change of concentration C with time; the integral accumulates a rate over time. A balance on a well-mixed tank is dM/dt = in − out + generation, where M is mass or moles. For a first-order decay with no inflow, dC/dt = −kC. Separating variables gives C = C0e^(−kt). Example: C0 = 1 mol/L, k = 0.1 min⁻¹, t = 10 min, so C = e^(−1) = 0.368 mol/L. The same mathematics appears in material and energy balances.

sections.heading: Linear algebra
sections.text: Linear algebra solves sets of linear equations. A material balance around several units gives Ax = b, where A holds coefficients, x the unknown flows or concentrations, and b the known inputs. The determinant, a number from A, shows whether a unique solution exists; if it is zero, there is no unique solution. Example: x + y = 10 and 2x − y = 2 give x = 4, y = 6. Matrices also describe linear transformations and are used in regression and process control.

sections.heading: Differential equations
sections.text: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) contains derivatives with respect to a single independent variable. First-order ODEs model tanks, reactors and cooling; second-order ODEs model vibrating systems. The Laplace transform changes a time function f(t) into F(s), turning an ODE into algebra. Key rules: L{1} = 1/s, L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a), and L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0). Solve the algebra, then invert to return to time. Linear ODEs with constant coefficients are common.

sections.heading: Series and vectors
sections.text: Series approximate functions. The Taylor series writes f(x) near a point as a sum of derivatives; e^x = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … . This gives a straight-line approximation to nonlinear rate laws for small changes. Vector calculus uses vectors for direction and magnitude. The gradient points to the steepest increase; divergence measures net outflow from a point; curl measures rotation. These ideas describe velocity, heat flux and mass flux fields in transport problems.

keyPoints: A balance on a well-mixed system is dM/dt = in − out + generation.
For first-order decay, dC/dt = −kC gives C = C0e^(−kt).
A linear system Ax = b has a unique solution when det A is not zero.
The Laplace transform rules L{1} = 1/s, L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a) and L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0) turn ODEs into algebra.
The Taylor series e^x = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … gives a straight-line approximation to nonlinear rate laws for small changes.
Gradient, divergence and curl describe steepest increase, net outflow and rotation in transport fields.

en.title: General chemistry for engineers
en.short: Atoms and bonding, the mole and stoichiometry, pH, redox, equilibrium and solution concentration.

sections.heading: Atoms and bonding
sections.text:
An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells. The proton count, the atomic number Z, fixes the element. The outer, or valence, electrons control bonding.

Ionic bonding transfers electrons: sodium gives one to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻, held by electrostatic attraction. Covalent bonding shares electrons, as in H₂O. Metallic bonding shares electrons across a lattice. Bond type helps predict melting point, solubility and reactivity.

sections.heading: Stoichiometry
sections.text:
Stoichiometry uses the balanced equation and the mole. One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant; its mass in grams is the molar mass.

Example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Burning 8 g of methane (molar mass 16 g/mol) is 8 ÷ 16 = 0.5 mol. It needs 0.5 × 2 = 1 mol of O₂, that is 32 g. It gives 0.5 mol CO₂ (44 g/mol, so 22 g) and 1 mol H₂O (18 g). Mass balances: 8 + 32 = 40 = 22 + 18. The limiting reactant sets the yield.

sections.heading: Acids, bases and pH
sections.text:
An acid donates a proton and a base accepts one (Brønsted). Strong acids ionise fully; weak acids only partly. pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], with [H⁺] in mol/dm³.

Example: 0.01 mol/dm³ HCl is strong, so [H⁺] = 0.01 and pH = −log₁₀(0.01) = 2. A weak acid at the same concentration, 1% ionised, gives [H⁺] = 0.0001 and pH = 4.

sections.heading: Redox, equilibrium, solutions
sections.text:
Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. They occur together, and the electrons lost equal those gained.

At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stop changing. For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, K = [C]^c[D]^d ÷ ([A]^a[B]^b). K changes with temperature. Le Chatelier’s principle says a change in concentration, pressure or temperature shifts the position to oppose it.

Molarity is moles of solute per dm³ of solution. Ionic solids dissolve into ions that carry current; solubility limits how much dissolves.

keyPoints: One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, and its mass in grams is the molar mass.
Balance the equation, convert to moles, apply the mole ratios; the limiting reactant sets the yield.
pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], with [H⁺] in mol/dm³.
Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain; both happen together.
At equilibrium K = [products]^coefficients ÷ [reactants]^coefficients, and K depends on temperature.
Molarity = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in dm³.

en.title: Hydrocarbons, functional groups and simple organic reactions
en.short: Hydrocarbons, functional groups, isomerism and simple reactions in fuels, polymers and medicines.

sections.heading: Hydrocarbons
sections.text: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes have only single bonds and are saturated; their general formula is CnH2n+2. They are the main molecules in natural gas, petrol, diesel and kerosene, and they burn to release heat. Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) and are unsaturated; with one double bond their formula is CnH2n. Ethene makes polyethene. Aromatic compounds contain a benzene ring, a six-carbon ring with delocalised π electrons. Benzene is stable because its electrons are shared around the ring.

sections.heading: Functional groups
sections.text: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a family of organic compounds its characteristic reactions. The hydroxyl group (-OH) makes an alcohol, such as ethanol. The carbonyl group (C=O) makes an aldehyde or ketone. The carboxyl group (-COOH) makes a carboxylic acid, such as ethanoic acid. An ester forms when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol. Amines contain nitrogen, amides contain a carbonyl next to nitrogen, and halogenoalkanes contain a halogen. These groups control solubility, boiling point and reactivity, so they matter in solvents and drug design.

sections.heading: Isomerism and reactions
sections.text: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Structural isomers differ in which atoms are joined. Geometric isomers differ around a C=C bond, giving cis and trans forms. Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Alkanes mainly undergo substitution, for example with chlorine in ultraviolet light. Alkenes undergo addition, such as adding hydrogen or bromine across C=C. Aromatics also undergo substitution more readily than addition. Alcohols can be oxidised: primary alcohols give aldehydes and then acids, secondary alcohols give ketones. They can also be eliminated to alkenes. These reaction types let chemists build larger molecules.

sections.heading: Industrial links
sections.text: In industry, alkanes supply fuels, alkenes make polymers, and aromatic and oxygenated compounds serve as solvents and intermediates. Ethanol is a solvent, ethanoic acid is an acid, and ethyl ethanoate is an ester used as a solvent. Their functional groups explain the different uses. In pharmaceutical processes, these groups guide synthesis and control how a drug dissolves.

keyPoints: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen; alkanes are saturated with formula CnH2n+2.
Alkenes have a C=C double bond and formula CnH2n for one double bond; they undergo addition.
Aromatic compounds contain a stable benzene ring and tend to undergo substitution.
Functional groups such as -OH, C=O, -COOH, ester, amine and halogen control properties and reactions.
Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure, geometry or optical arrangement.
Alkanes undergo substitution, alkenes addition, and alcohols oxidation or elimination; these reactions link organic chemistry to fuels, polymers, solvents and medicines.

en.title: Physical chemistry: gases, solutions and kinetics
en.short: Gas laws, solution properties, phase behaviour, simple electrochemistry, reaction rates and equilibrium.

sections.heading: Gases
sections.text: An ideal gas obeys pV = nRT, where n is moles, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T is absolute temperature. It assumes point molecules with no forces between them; real gases approach this at low pressure and high temperature. Dalton’s law gives the total pressure of a non-reacting mixture as the sum of partial pressures, p_i = y_i p. Example: 2.0 mol at 300 K in 0.050 m³ gives p = 2.0 × 8.314 × 300 ÷ 0.050 = 99,768 Pa ≈ 99.8 kPa.

sections.heading: Solutions and phases
sections.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture. Ideal solutions obey Raoult’s law: p_i = x_i p_i*, where x_i is mole fraction and p_i* is the pure vapour pressure. Real solutions deviate, so activity is used. Colligative properties depend on particle number: vapour pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure. Phase diagrams show which phase is stable. At phase equilibrium, temperature, pressure and chemical potential of each component are equal in both phases. The lever rule gives phase amounts.

sections.heading: Electrochemistry
sections.text: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical work; an electrolytic cell does the reverse, using electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. Oxidation loses electrons at the anode; reduction gains them at the cathode. Cell potential E is the difference between electrode potentials. The Nernst equation corrects for concentration: E = E° − (RT ÷ nF) ln Q, where n is electrons transferred, F ≈ 96,485 C mol⁻¹ and Q is the reaction quotient. At 298 K, E = E° − (0.0592 ÷ n) log Q. A positive E means the cell reaction is spontaneous.

sections.heading: Rates and equilibrium
sections.text: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time. A rate law has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; the orders m and n come from experiment, not the balanced equation. The rate constant usually rises with temperature: k = A exp(−Ea ÷ RT), where Ea is activation energy. At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal. The equilibrium constant K is a ratio of activities (concentrations in dilute solution). K changes with temperature, not with pressure or initial amounts. Le Chatelier’s principle predicts the shift after a disturbance.

keyPoints: Ideal gas law: pV = nRT, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T in kelvin.
Dalton’s law: total pressure is the sum of partial pressures, p_i = y_i p.
Raoult’s law for ideal solutions is p_i = x_i p_i*; colligative properties depend on particle number.
Nernst equation: E = E° − (RT ÷ nF) ln Q; at 298 K the factor RT/F × ln 10 is about 0.0592 V.
Rate law: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, with orders found by experiment; k usually follows k = A exp(−Ea ÷ RT).
At equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal; K depends on temperature, not pressure or initial amounts.

en.title: Engineering physics: mechanics, waves, heat and electricity
en.short: Newtonian mechanics, work and energy, waves, heat and basic electricity for process equipment.

sections.heading: Mechanics and energy
sections.text: Newtonian mechanics describes motion with force, mass and acceleration. Newton’s second law is F = ma for constant mass; weight is W = mg, with g about 9.81 m/s². Momentum p = mv is conserved when no external force acts. Work is force times displacement along the force, W = Fd. Kinetic energy is ½mv²; gravitational potential energy near the Earth is mgh. Energy is conserved; power is work per second, P = W ÷ t. Example: lifting a 2 kg block 3 m needs mgh = 2 × 9.81 × 3 = 58.86 J. Over 2 s, power is 58.86 ÷ 2 = 29.43 W.

sections.heading: Waves
sections.text: A wave carries energy through a medium or space without carrying matter. Wavelength λ is crest-to-crest distance; frequency f is cycles per second; speed v = fλ. Amplitude is maximum displacement. Transverse waves oscillate across the travel direction; longitudinal waves oscillate along it. Superposition adds displacements, giving interference. Example: sound at 170 Hz in air at about 340 m/s has λ = 340 ÷ 170 = 2 m.

sections.heading: Heat
sections.text: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy. Specific heat capacity c is energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K: Q = mcΔT. Heat that changes temperature like this is called sensible heat. Latent heat L is energy per kilogram for a phase change: Q = mL. Conduction follows Q ÷ t = kAΔT ÷ L, where k is thermal conductivity, A area and L thickness. Convection moves heat with a fluid; radiation needs no medium.

sections.heading: Basic electricity
sections.text: Electric charge is measured in coulombs. Current I is charge flow per second in amperes. Potential difference V is energy per unit charge in volts. Resistance R in ohms limits current; for many conductors at constant temperature Ohm’s law gives V = IR. Electrical power is P = VI = I²R. This links to electrical heating and instrument signals. In series, currents are equal; in parallel, voltages are equal.

keyPoints: Newton’s second law is F = ma, and weight is W = mg.
Work is W = Fd; kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential energy near Earth is mgh.
Wave speed is v = fλ, where f is frequency and λ is wavelength.
Heat transfer by conduction follows Q ÷ t = kAΔT ÷ L, and sensible heat is Q = mcΔT.
Latent heat for a phase change is Q = mL.
Ohm’s law is V = IR, and electrical power is P = VI = I²R.

en.title: Computing and numerical methods for engineers
en.short: Programming, spreadsheets and numerical methods for solving engineering problems.

sections.heading: Programming basics
sections.text:
A program is a list of instructions a computer carries out. The basics are variables (named stores for values), data types (integer, real, text, logical), sequence, selection (if), iteration (loops), functions and arrays. Pseudocode plans the logic before coding. Test small cases and check units. Floating point numbers are rounded, so compare two real numbers with a small tolerance, not exact equality.

Write readable code with clear names and comments.

sections.heading: Spreadsheets
sections.text: Spreadsheets store numbers in cells and calculate with formulas such as =A1*B1. Use absolute references ($B$1) for constants, built-in functions for sums and averages, and charts to see trends. Goal Seek finds an input that gives a chosen result. Spreadsheets suit small models, quick checks and data tables. Keep assumptions in labelled cells and document them; large or safety-critical models need tested code.

sections.heading: Roots and interpolation
sections.text:
Root finding solves f(x)=0. Bisection needs a sign change between two points and halves the interval each step. Newton-Raphson uses x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)); it is fast but can fail if the derivative is zero or the start is poor.

Example: solve x² − 2 = 0 from x0 = 1. x1 = 1 − (−1) ÷ 2 = 1.5. x2 = 1.5 − 0.25 ÷ 3 = 1.416667, close to √2.

Linear interpolation estimates between points: y = y1 + (x − x1)(y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1).

sections.heading: Integration and ODEs
sections.text:
Numerical integration estimates area under a curve. The trapezium rule is I ≈ (h ÷ 2)[f(x0) + 2f(x1) + ... + f(xn)]. For f(x)=x² from 0 to 1 with h=0.5: I ≈ 0.25[0 + 2(0.25) + 1] = 0.375; exact value is 1/3 ≈ 0.3333.

An ordinary differential equation (ODE) relates a function to its derivative. Euler’s method steps forward: y(x+h) ≈ y + h f(x,y). For y′ = y, y(0)=1 and h=0.1: y(0.1) ≈ 1.1, then y(0.2) ≈ 1.21. Exact e^0.2 ≈ 1.2214. Smaller h usually improves accuracy but costs more computation.

keyPoints: Bisection halves a sign-changing interval; Newton-Raphson uses x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)).
Linear interpolation: y = y1 + (x − x1)(y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1).
Trapezium rule: I ≈ (h ÷ 2)[f(x0) + 2f(x1) + ... + f(xn)].
Euler’s method: y(x+h) ≈ y + h f(x,y).
Test programs on small cases and compare numerical answers with exact or trusted values.
Spreadsheets suit small models; use absolute references for constants and document assumptions.

en.title: Engineering drawing and process diagrams
en.short: Orthographic views, dimensioning, sketching, PFDs and P&IDs with symbols and line types.

sections.heading: Orthographic views
sections.text: Orthographic projection shows a three-dimensional object as separate two-dimensional views, usually front, top and side. Projectors are parallel, so a face parallel to the viewing plane keeps true shape and size. First-angle projection places the left view on the right; third-angle places it on the left. The projection symbol in the title block tells which is used. Visible outlines are solid, hidden edges dashed, centre lines long-short dashes. Read the title block, scale and projection symbol first.

sections.heading: Dimensioning and sketching
sections.text: Dimensioning gives size and location. Extension lines start with a small gap from the object, dimension lines carry the value, and arrowheads touch the extension lines. Give each dimension once, on the view that shows the feature clearly. Tolerances state the permitted variation. Sketches are freehand drawings in correct proportion, not to scale; finished drawings use a stated scale such as 1:20. Read a drawing by following views, centre lines, dimensions and notes together. Check units and the standard named in the title block, because conventions differ between countries and companies.

sections.heading: Process diagrams
sections.text:
A process flow diagram (PFD) shows the main equipment and material flow through a plant. It uses symbols for vessels, pumps, compressors, heat exchangers and reactors, with arrows for flow direction. It shows stream numbers and key temperatures and pressures, but not every pipe, valve or instrument. A PFD is for understanding the process, not for construction. Symbols vary, so read the legend.

A piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) adds piping, valves, instruments and control loops. Tags identify items: P-101 is a pump, E-101 a heat exchanger, FT-101 a flow transmitter, TIC-101 a temperature indicating controller. Line types distinguish piping from signal lines; utility lines are usually identified by labels or line numbers. Conventions differ, so read the legend. Case: feed leaves tank T-101, passes pump P-101 and heater E-101 to reactor R-101. The PFD shows this path; the P&ID adds line size, block valves and TIC-101 controlling the heater. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration; drawing standards are set by the client and may follow ISO or company rules.

keyPoints: Orthographic projection uses parallel projectors to give true-shape views; first-angle and third-angle place views differently.
Dimension drawings with extension lines, dimension lines and tolerances, giving each dimension once.
A PFD shows main equipment and material flow, not every pipe or instrument.
A P&ID adds piping, valves, instruments and control loops, using tags and a legend.
Read the title block, scale, projection symbol and legend before interpreting any drawing.
Drawing standards and symbols vary by country and company; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration, but the project standard is set by the client.

en.title: Introduction to chemical engineering: role, units and safety
en.short: The chemical engineer’s role, units and dimensions, process variables, unit operations, flowsheets and safety.

sections.heading: The engineer’s role
sections.text: Chemical engineers design, operate and improve processes that turn raw materials into useful products. They work from laboratory scale to full plant scale. Their aim is a process that is safe, reliable, economical and clean. They use balances, thermodynamics, transport and reaction knowledge, but this summary only maps the discipline.

sections.heading: Units and dimensions
sections.text:
A dimension is the physical kind of a quantity: mass (M), length (L), time (T) or temperature (Θ). A unit is the agreed amount used to measure it. SI base units include the kilogram, metre, second, kelvin and mole. Derived units include the newton (kg·m/s²), pascal (N/m²) and watt (J/s).

Equations must be dimensionally homogeneous: both sides have the same dimensions, and terms added together must match. Convert data to one consistent set of units before calculating.

Example: density 800 kg/m³ and volume flow 0.002 m³/s give mass flow = 800 × 0.002 = 1.6 kg/s. Units: (kg/m³)(m³/s) = kg/s.

sections.heading: Process variables and flowsheets
sections.text: Process variables are the measurable quantities that describe a stream or equipment: flow rate, composition, temperature, pressure, level, density and viscosity. A flowsheet is a diagram of the process. A block flowsheet shows the main steps; a process flow diagram adds equipment and stream data; a piping and instrumentation diagram adds instruments and control. Unit operations are physical steps such as mixing, heating, filtration and distillation. Unit processes are chemical steps.

sections.heading: Safety and responsibility
sections.text:
Chemical plants can contain flammable, toxic or high-pressure materials. Safety is therefore a design duty, not an afterthought: choose safer materials and conditions, provide relief and control systems, and review hazards before operation.

Professional registration is country-specific. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering practice. Other countries have their own bodies, codes and standards, so check the current official source rather than assuming one country’s rules apply everywhere. Ethical duties include protecting the public, being honest about competence and results, and reducing environmental harm.

keyPoints: Chemical engineers design and operate processes that are safe, economical and clean.
Dimensions are physical kinds such as M, L, T and Θ; units are the agreed measures.
Equations must be dimensionally homogeneous, and data must be converted to consistent units.
Mass flow = density × volumetric flow; for example 800 kg/m³ × 0.002 m³/s = 1.6 kg/s.
Unit operations are physical steps; unit processes are chemical steps; flowsheets map their sequence.
Safety is a design duty, and professional registration and codes differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Material and energy balances
en.short: Boundaries, steady and unsteady mass balances, recycle, purge, combustion and energy balances.

sections.heading: System boundaries
sections.text: A material balance starts with a system boundary around the equipment or plant. Streams crossing it are inputs and outputs. The general balance is accumulation = in − out + generation − consumption. For total mass, generation and consumption are zero in most processes. For each species, reaction can generate or consume it. At steady state accumulation is zero, so in + generation = out + consumption. Unsteady balances keep accumulation, as in filling or batch operations.

sections.heading: Recycle, bypass, purge
sections.text: A recycle stream returns part of an outlet to an earlier point. It raises overall conversion when a reaction is limited by equilibrium or low per-pass conversion, but inerts entering with the feed can build up in the loop. A purge removes a stream to keep inerts at a chosen level. A bypass sends part of a stream around a unit, often to control temperature or composition. Balances around mixing point and splitter are needed.

sections.heading: Reacting and combustion
sections.text: For a reaction, use the stoichiometric equation and extent or species balances. In combustion, theoretical oxygen converts fuel completely to CO2 and H2O. Excess air = (actual air − theoretical air) ÷ theoretical air × 100%. Example: 100 mol/s methane needs 200 mol/s O2: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. With 20% excess, O2 supplied = 240 mol/s. Taking air as 21 mol% O2, air = 240 ÷ 0.21 = 1143 mol/s.

sections.heading: Energy and combined
sections.text: Enthalpy H = U + PV. For steady flow with negligible kinetic and potential energy, Q − W = Σ out nH − Σ in nH, where Q is heat added, W is work done by the system. Sensible heat at constant cp is m cp ΔT. Heat of reaction is the enthalpy change when stoichiometric amounts react; negative ΔH means heat is released. Combined problems use material balances to fix flows and energy balances to find Q, W or temperature. Check units and reference states.

keyPoints: General mass balance: accumulation = in − out + generation − consumption; at steady state accumulation is zero.
For total mass in ordinary processes, generation and consumption are zero; component balances include reaction.
Recycle raises overall conversion but inerts entering with the feed can build up in the loop; purge controls inerts and bypass routes part of a stream around a unit.
Combustion: theoretical O2 follows stoichiometry; excess air = (actual air − theoretical air) ÷ theoretical air × 100%.
Steady energy balance: Q − W = Σ out nH − Σ in nH; sensible heat = m cp ΔT.
Heat of reaction is the enthalpy change for stoichiometric reaction; negative ΔH means heat released.

en.title: Chemical engineering thermodynamics
en.short: First and second laws, PVT behaviour, equations of state, fugacity, phase and reaction equilibrium.

sections.heading: Laws and PVT
sections.text:
First law: ΔU = Q − W for a closed system (U internal energy, Q heat added, W work done by system). Enthalpy H = U + PV suits constant pressure. Second law: entropy S of an isolated system cannot fall. Gibbs energy G = H − TS gives spontaneity at fixed T and P: ΔG < 0 means forward. Chemical potential μ, the partial molar Gibbs energy, drives phase transfer.

PVT behaviour links P, V and T. Ideal gas law PV = nRT is a low-pressure limit. Real gases deviate because molecules attract and occupy volume. An equation of state (EOS) models this. Van der Waals: (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, with a and b for attraction and size. Cubic EOS such as Peng-Robinson use critical properties and the acentric factor, a parameter for molecular shape. Compressibility Z = PV/(nRT) measures non-ideality.

sections.heading: Fugacity and phase equilibria
sections.text: Fugacity f is a corrected pressure that makes the chemical potential of a real gas equal to that of an ideal gas: μ = μ° + RT ln(f/f°). For a liquid, activity a = f/f° and the activity coefficient γ = a/x, where x is mole fraction. At phase equilibrium, fugacity or chemical potential is equal in each phase. Vapour-liquid equilibrium is often written y_i P φ_i = x_i γ_i P_sat,i, where y_i and x_i are vapour and liquid mole fractions, φ_i a fugacity coefficient and P_sat,i the saturation pressure. Activity models describe non-ideal mixtures.

sections.heading: Reaction equilibrium
sections.text: For a reaction, ΔG° = −RT ln K, where ΔG° is the standard Gibbs energy change and K the equilibrium constant. At equilibrium K = Π a_i^ν_i, with ν_i the stoichiometric number, positive for products and negative for reactants. Example: for A ⇌ B at 298 K, if ΔG° = −5.00 kJ/mol, then K = exp(−ΔG°/RT) = exp(5000 ÷ (8.314 × 298)) = exp(2.018) = 7.52. Thus a_B/a_A ≈ 7.52 at equilibrium. Design uses EOS and activity models to relate K to equilibrium compositions and phase amounts.

keyPoints: First law for a closed system: ΔU = Q − W, with W work done by the system.
Second law: entropy of an isolated system cannot fall; at fixed T and P, ΔG < 0 means a process can go forward.
Van der Waals EOS: (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT; Z = PV/(nRT) measures non-ideality.
Fugacity gives real-gas chemical potential: μ = μ° + RT ln(f/f°).
At phase equilibrium, fugacity or chemical potential is equal in each phase; VLE often uses y_i P φ_i = x_i γ_i P_sat,i.
Reaction equilibrium: ΔG° = −RT ln K and K = Π a_i^ν_i.

en.title: Fluid mechanics for chemical engineers: pipe flow and pumping
en.short: Fluid properties, hydrostatics, energy equations, pipe friction, pumps and flow measurement for sizing lines.

sections.heading: Properties and hydrostatics
sections.text:
Fluid properties include density ρ, viscosity μ and vapour pressure. Kinematic viscosity is ν = μ ÷ ρ. Newtonian fluids have shear stress proportional to shear rate; non-Newtonian fluids do not.

Hydrostatics treats fluids at rest. Pressure rises with depth: p = p0 + ρgh. The same level in a connected static fluid has equal pressure. This explains manometers and tank-wall force.

sections.heading: Energy and friction
sections.text:
Continuity for steady flow is ρ1A1v1 = ρ2A2v2, or Q = Av for constant density. Bernoulli for frictionless incompressible flow is p ÷ ρg + v² ÷ 2g + z = constant. The energy equation adds pump head Hp and subtracts friction head hf and minor loss hm.

Reynolds number Re = ρvD ÷ μ predicts regime. Laminar pipe flow is usually Re below about 2000 and turbulent above about 4000. Laminar f = 64 ÷ Re. Turbulent f depends on Re and relative roughness ε ÷ D, from the Moody chart or Colebrook equation.

Darcy-Weisbach: hf = f(L ÷ D)(v² ÷ 2g). Fittings add hm = K v² ÷ 2g.

Example: water, D = 0.05 m, v = 2 m/s, L = 30 m, f = 0.02, μ = 0.001 Pa·s. Re = 1000 × 2 × 0.05 ÷ 0.001 = 100,000. hf = 0.02 × (30 ÷ 0.05) × (2² ÷ 19.62) = 2.45 m.

sections.heading: Pumps, measurement and sizing
sections.text:
Pump head H is energy per unit weight. Pump power is P = ρgQH ÷ η, where η is efficiency. Net positive suction head (NPSH) available must exceed required NPSH to avoid cavitation; the maker gives required NPSH. Orifice plates, venturi meters and rotameters measure flow; their readings rely on meter coefficients from standards or calibration.

To size a line, choose a practical velocity, calculate D = √(4Q ÷ πv), select the next standard pipe size, then compute hf, hm and pump head. Design codes and limits differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates registration. Check current local code and maker data.

keyPoints: Pressure in a static fluid rises with depth: p = p0 + ρgh.
Continuity for constant density is Q = Av; for steady flow ρ1A1v1 = ρ2A2v2.
Bernoulli: p ÷ ρg + v² ÷ 2g + z is constant for frictionless incompressible flow; the energy equation adds pump head and subtracts friction.
Reynolds number Re = ρvD ÷ μ separates laminar, transitional and turbulent flow.
Darcy-Weisbach friction head is hf = f(L ÷ D)(v² ÷ 2g); fittings add K v² ÷ 2g.
Pump power is P = ρgQH ÷ η; size pipes from D = √(4Q ÷ πv) and check NPSH.

en.title: Heat transfer and exchanger design
en.short: Conduction, convection, radiation, U, LMTD and effectiveness, fouling, boiling and condensation.

sections.heading: Modes and resistances
sections.text: Heat crosses a surface by three modes. Conduction is energy diffusion without bulk motion: q = −kA dT/dx, where k is thermal conductivity. Convection moves heat between a surface and a fluid: q = hA(Ts − Tf), where h is the heat transfer coefficient. Radiation is electromagnetic emission; a black body emits q = σAT⁴, with σ the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. For a plane wall between two fluids, resistances in series give 1/UA = 1/(h1A) + L/(kA) + 1/(h2A). U is the overall heat transfer coefficient.

sections.heading: Fouling and U
sections.text: Fouling is a deposit of scale, coke or biological film; it adds resistance Rf (m²·K/W). For unit area, 1/U = 1/h1 + Rf1 + L/k + Rf2 + 1/h2. Example: h1 = 500, h2 = 1000 W/(m²·K), L/k = 0.0005, total Rf = 0.0002 m²·K/W. Then 1/U = 0.002 + 0.0005 + 0.0002 + 0.001 = 0.0037, so U = 270 W/(m²·K). Fouling allowances and design codes vary by country and service; use current official values.

sections.heading: Exchanger sizing
sections.text: For an exchanger, q = UAΔTlm, with ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2). For multipass units multiply by F ≤ 1. The effectiveness method avoids trial and error: ε = q/qmax, qmax = Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in), and NTU = UA/Cmin. Effectiveness depends on NTU, the flow arrangement and Cr = Cmin/Cmax. Example in counterflow: hot 150 to 90 °C, cold 30 to 70 °C gives ΔT1 = 80 K, ΔT2 = 60 K, ΔTlm = 20/ln(80/60) = 69.5 K.

sections.heading: Boiling and condensation
sections.text: Boiling in a pool passes from natural convection to nucleate boiling, where h is high, then critical heat flux, where burnout can occur, then transition and film boiling with much lower h. Condensation is filmwise, described by Nusselt theory, or dropwise, which gives higher h. Design keeps boiling below critical heat flux and removes non-condensable gases.

keyPoints: Conduction is q = −kA dT/dx, convection is q = hA(Ts − Tf), and a black body radiates q = σAT⁴.
For a plane wall, 1/U = 1/h1 + L/k + Rf + 1/h2 per unit area, so the largest resistance controls U.
Fouling adds resistance and lowers U; allowances and design codes vary by country and service, so check current official values.
For an exchanger, q = UAΔTlm with ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2), and multipass units need F ≤ 1.
The effectiveness method uses ε = q/qmax, qmax = Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in), and NTU = UA/Cmin.
Boiling has a critical heat flux; film boiling and non-condensable gases sharply reduce heat transfer.

en.title: Mass transfer fundamentals
en.short: Diffusion, Fick’s law, mass transfer coefficients, interphase transfer and contact analysis.

sections.heading: Diffusion and Fick’s law
sections.text:
Diffusion is net movement of a species down a concentration gradient. For dilute mixtures, Fick’s law gives molar flux J_A = −D_AB dC_A/dx, where D_AB is diffusivity (m²/s) and x is distance. The sign shows flow down the gradient. Concentrated mixtures add a bulk-flow term. Gas diffusivity rises with temperature and falls with pressure; liquid diffusivity depends on temperature and viscosity.

Example: D_AB = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, C falls by 60 mol/m³ over 3 mm.
J_A = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 60 ÷ 0.003 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol/(m²·s).

sections.heading: Mass transfer coefficients
sections.text: The interfacial gradient is hard to measure, so engineers use a mass transfer coefficient k_c. For dilute transfer, N_A = k_c (C_A,bulk − C_A,interface), with k_c in m/s. It lumps film behaviour into one value. Correlations give k_c from flow, diffusivity and geometry. If k_c = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ m/s and the concentration difference is 60 mol/m³, N_A = 1.2 × 10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). Coefficients may use mole fraction or pressure, so check the driving-force units.

sections.heading: Interphase transfer
sections.text: Solute moves between phases until equilibrium. For dilute systems the equilibrium line is often y* = m x. The two-film theory pictures a stagnant film on each side. At steady state the film fluxes are equal, so resistances add in series, weighted by equilibrium. The resulting overall coefficient K_ov describes both films. The slower film controls the rate; a large m can make one phase’s resistance dominate.

sections.heading: Staged and continuous contact
sections.text: Staged contact repeats mixing and separation, as on a tray. Ideal stages come from equilibrium and operating lines; stage efficiency corrects for incomplete contact. Continuous contact, as in a packed column, uses the number of transfer units NTU = ∫ dC/(C − C*) and height of a transfer unit HTU = G/K_a, where G is the molar flow rate per unit area and a is interfacial area per packed volume. Packed height is Z = NTU × HTU. NTU measures separation difficulty; HTU measures equipment performance. Design codes differ by country; check the local code.

keyPoints: Fick’s law for dilute mixtures is J_A = −D_AB dC_A/dx.
Mass transfer coefficient: N_A = k_c (C_A,bulk − C_A,interface).
Gas diffusivity rises with temperature and falls with pressure.
Interphase film resistances add in series; the slower film controls.
Staged contact uses equilibrium and operating lines with stage efficiency.
Continuous contact uses Z = NTU × HTU, with NTU = ∫ dC/(C − C*).

en.title: Distillation: equilibrium stages and column design
en.short: Vapour liquid equilibrium, McCabe-Thiele, reflux, stage efficiency, batch and continuous distillation, azeotropes.

sections.heading: Vapour liquid equilibrium
sections.text: At equilibrium the vapour and liquid compositions are related by the equilibrium curve. For an ideal binary mixture, Raoult’s law gives y = αx ÷ (1 + (α − 1)x) when relative volatility α is constant. The bubble point is the temperature at which the first vapour forms; the dew point is where the first liquid forms. Real mixtures need measured data because activity coefficients are not one.

sections.heading: McCabe-Thiele method
sections.text:
Simple distillation uses one equilibrium stage. Fractional distillation uses reflux and many stages. McCabe-Thiele is a graphical stage count for binary mixtures. Plot the equilibrium curve and the operating lines. The rectifying line is y = (R ÷ (R + 1))x + xD ÷ (R + 1), where R = L ÷ D is the reflux ratio. The stripping line and the feed q-line, which passes through the feed composition, complete the construction. Step between the operating line and the equilibrium curve.

Example: xD = 0.95, R = 2, α = 2.5. The rectifying line is y = 0.667x + 0.317. From xD, horizontal to equilibrium: x = 0.95 ÷ (2.5 − 1.5 × 0.95) = 0.884. Vertical to the operating line: y = 0.667 × 0.884 + 0.317 = 0.906. One theoretical stage takes x from 0.95 to 0.884.

sections.heading: Reflux and efficiency
sections.text: More reflux means fewer stages but more reboiler and condenser duty. Minimum reflux needs infinite stages; total reflux gives the minimum stages. Stage efficiency η compares theoretical stages to actual stages: actual stages = theoretical stages ÷ η. If 8 theoretical stages are needed at η = 0.60, actual stages = 8 ÷ 0.60 = 13.3, so use 14. Efficiencies depend on the system and are often from correlations or tests.

sections.heading: Operation and azeotropes
sections.text: Continuous columns run at steady state with a feed, distillate and bottoms. Batch distillation charges a pot and changes composition with time. An azeotrope boils at constant composition, so ordinary distillation cannot pass it. Pressure change or an entrainer may help. Mechanical design follows national pressure-vessel codes.

keyPoints: At equilibrium, y = αx ÷ (1 + (α − 1)x) for constant relative volatility α.
The rectifying operating line is y = (R ÷ (R + 1))x + xD ÷ (R + 1), with R = L ÷ D.
McCabe-Thiele counts theoretical stages by stepping between the operating line and the equilibrium curve.
More reflux reduces the stages needed but raises energy use; minimum reflux needs infinite stages.
Actual stages = theoretical stages ÷ stage efficiency.
An azeotrope has the same vapour and liquid composition and cannot be separated by ordinary distillation.

en.title: Absorption, extraction, adsorption, drying and membrane separations
en.short: Design of absorption, extraction, adsorption, drying and membrane units from equilibrium and mass transfer.

sections.heading: Absorption and extraction
sections.text:
Gas absorption removes a soluble gas from a gas mixture into a liquid. Design uses Henry’s law, p = Hx for dilute solutions, and an operating line from a mass balance. The driving force is the gap between the operating and equilibrium lines. Packed towers are sized with height and number of transfer units, or with an overall mass transfer coefficient and column volume.

Liquid-liquid extraction moves a solute between two immiscible liquids. The partition coefficient K = y/x sets equilibrium. Mass ratios are used because carrier and solvent flows stay nearly constant. Mixer-settlers or columns provide stages.

sections.heading: Adsorption and drying
sections.text: Adsorption binds solute onto a solid surface. Equilibrium isotherms such as Langmuir and Freundlich, and breakthrough curves, size the bed. Drying removes moisture by evaporation. The drying curve has a constant-rate period and a falling-rate period. Design uses heat and mass balances, psychrometric data and measured drying rates. Adsorption suits dilute streams; drying suits solids.

sections.heading: Membranes
sections.text: Membrane separations use a semipermeable barrier. Flux is driving force divided by resistance. For reverse osmosis, water flux J = A(Δp − Δπ), where Δπ is osmotic pressure difference. Modules are sized from area = flow ÷ flux. Fouling and concentration polarisation reduce performance.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
100 kg feed contains 20 kg solute in 80 kg carrier. Fresh solvent is 100 kg and solute-free. Equilibrium is Y = 2X, where X and Y are kg solute per kg carrier and per kg solvent.
Feed X0 = 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25.
Balance: 80(0.25 − X1) = 100(Y1 − 0), and Y1 = 2X1.
20 − 80X1 = 200X1, so X1 = 0.0714 and Y1 = 0.1429.
Solute extracted = 100 × 0.1429 = 14.29 kg, or 71.4%.

keyPoints: Absorption design uses Henry’s law and an operating line; the driving force is the gap to equilibrium.
Extraction equilibrium is K = y/x, and mass balances are best written in mass ratios.
Adsorption beds are sized from isotherms and breakthrough curves; drying from heat and mass balances and drying-rate data.
Membrane flux is driving force ÷ resistance, and area = flow ÷ flux.
In the worked example, 14.29 kg of 20 kg solute is extracted, or 71.4%.
Use a consistent basis and check units; equilibrium data vary with temperature and system.

en.title: Chemical reaction engineering: rates, reactors and catalysis
en.short: Rate laws, batch, CSTR and PFR sizing, multiple reactions, non-isothermal operation and catalysis.

sections.heading: Rate laws and data
sections.text:
A rate law links reaction rate to concentrations, often −r_A = k C_A^n for an irreversible power-law reaction. k is the rate constant and n the order. The Arrhenius equation k = A exp(−E/RT) shows strong temperature dependence; E is activation energy and A the pre-exponential factor.

Kinetic data come from batch experiments: measure C_A against time, then use the differential method (plot ln(−r_A) against ln C_A, slope n) or the integral method (test integrated forms).

sections.heading: Ideal reactors
sections.text:
Batch, continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) and plug flow reactor (PFR) are ideal models. For constant-volume batch, −dC_A/dt = −r_A. For a CSTR at steady state, V = F_A0 X ÷ (−r_A). For a PFR, V = F_A0 ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A). X is conversion and F_A0 is feed molar flow.

For a first-order liquid reaction, k = 0.1 min⁻¹, v0 = 10 L/min, X = 0.9:
CSTR: V = v0 X ÷ [k(1 − X)] = 10 × 0.9 ÷ (0.1 × 0.1) = 900 L
PFR: V = (v0 ÷ k) ln[1 ÷ (1 − X)] = 100 × ln 10 = 230 L
The PFR needs less volume because its average concentration, and so its rate, is higher; a CSTR runs at the low exit concentration throughout.

sections.heading: Multiple reactions
sections.text: With multiple reactions, selectivity and yield matter. Selectivity is desired product formed divided by undesired product formed; yield is desired product formed divided by A consumed. For parallel reactions, adjust concentration and temperature to favour the desired path. For series reactions such as A → D → U, D is an intermediate, so very high conversion destroys it; choose reactor and conditions to keep D.

sections.heading: Heat and catalysis
sections.text: Non-isothermal reactors need the energy balance with the rate law. In an adiabatic reactor (no heat exchange), temperature rises with conversion for an exothermic reaction and falls for an endothermic one, so k changes; a CSTR can show multiple steady states and ignition or extinction. Catalysis lowers activation energy by providing an alternative path; it does not change equilibrium. In heterogeneous catalysis the steps are external diffusion, pore diffusion, adsorption, surface reaction and desorption; the slowest step controls the observed rate. Catalyst deactivation must be allowed for.

keyPoints: Rate law: −r_A = k C_A^n, and k = A exp(−E/RT).
Constant-volume batch balance: −dC_A/dt = −r_A.
CSTR sizing: V = F_A0 X ÷ (−r_A); PFR sizing: V = F_A0 ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A).
For k = 0.1 min⁻¹, v0 = 10 L/min and X = 0.9, a first-order liquid reaction needs 900 L in a CSTR and 230 L in a PFR.
Selectivity and yield guide multiple reactions, and for A → D → U avoid over-conversion.
Catalysts lower activation energy and speed the approach to equilibrium but do not shift equilibrium.

en.title: Process control and instrumentation
en.short: Sensors, transmitters, valves, feedback, PID, stability, tuning and P&ID reading for chemical processes.

sections.heading: Sensors and transmitters
sections.text:
A sensor measures a process variable such as temperature, pressure, flow or level. A transmitter converts the sensor signal into a standard signal for the control system, commonly 4-20 mA or a digital fieldbus signal.

The 4 mA live zero lets the system detect a broken wire. Choose an instrument range that covers normal and upset conditions.

sections.heading: Valves and feedback
sections.text:
A control valve is the final control element. An actuator moves the stem, and a positioner holds the opening. Fail-safe action matters: on loss of air or power the valve should go to a safe position.

In feedback control the controller compares the measured variable (PV) with the setpoint (SP). The error is e = SP − PV. The controller output moves the valve to reduce e.

sections.heading: PID and stability
sections.text:
PID control adds three actions. Proportional action uP = Kp e responds to error. Integral action uI = Ki ∫e dt removes offset (steady error) but can slow the loop. Derivative action uD = Kd de/dt reacts to slope and amplifies noise. The output is u = uP + uI + uD.

A loop is stable if a bounded disturbance gives a bounded response that settles. Too much gain, dead time (delay) or lag can cause oscillation.

Example: Kp = 2, Ki = 0.5/s, Kd = 0.1 s, e = 4%, ∫e dt = 6 % s, de/dt = −0.5 %/s. Then u = 2×4 + 0.5×6 + 0.1×(−0.5) = 8 + 3 − 0.05 = 10.95%.

sections.heading: Tuning and P&IDs
sections.text:
Tuning sets Kp, Ki and Kd. Classic methods include Ziegler-Nichols and Cohen-Coon; model-based tuning uses a model. Tune safely with small setpoint changes.

A piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) shows equipment, pipes, instruments and signals. Read tags such as TIC (temperature indicating controller) and follow the signal from sensor to controller to valve. Symbols follow standards such as ISA and ISO; installation and registration rules are national. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration. Check standards and local rules.

keyPoints: A sensor measures the variable; a transmitter sends a standard signal, commonly 4-20 mA or digital.
In feedback control, error e = SP − PV, and the controller output drives the valve to reduce it.
PID output is u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt; integral removes steady offset and derivative reacts to slope.
A loop is stable when a bounded disturbance gives a bounded response that settles; too much gain or dead time causes oscillation.
Tune with safe, small setpoint changes using methods such as Ziegler-Nichols, Cohen-Coon or a process model.

On a P&ID, read instrument tags and follow the signal from sensor to controller to final control element; symbols follow standards such as ISA and ISO, while registration rules are national (COREN in Nigeria).

en.title: Particle technology and solids handling
en.short: Particle size, screening, comminution, fluidisation, filtration, sedimentation and solids conveying.

sections.heading: Particle size and distribution
sections.text: Particle size is usually an equivalent diameter: the diameter of a sphere with the same property, such as volume or settling rate. A powder is described by its size distribution, often from sieve analysis. The d50 is the median size; the spread shows how wide the distribution is. Irregular shape, agglomeration and moisture affect measured values, so report the method used.

sections.heading: Screening and comminution
sections.text: Screening separates particles by size as they pass through openings. Screen efficiency falls when particles are near the aperture size or when the bed is too thick. Comminution reduces size by crushing or grinding. Energy laws such as Rittinger, Kick and Bond relate energy to size reduction, but their constants are material-specific and must come from tests, not assumed.

sections.heading: Fluidisation and conveying
sections.text: Fluidisation suspends solid particles in an upward fluid. At the minimum fluidisation velocity, drag balances the buoyant particle weight, so the pressure drop equals the buoyant bed weight per area: ΔP = (1−ε)(ρs−ρf)gL, where ε is voidage. Beyond this, gas-fluidised beds bubble, and at much higher velocities particles are entrained (carried out of the bed). Solids are conveyed by belt, screw, bucket elevator or pneumatic line. Each has limits on distance, angle and material degradation.

sections.heading: Filtration and sedimentation
sections.text:
Filtration removes solids from a liquid through a porous medium. The solid cake that builds up on the medium adds resistance, so flow falls as the cake grows. Sedimentation separates particles by gravity. For dilute spherical particles, Stokes law gives v = (ρp−ρf)g d² ÷ (18μ). Example: a sand particle of d = 0.05 mm (5×10⁻⁵ m) in water, with ρp = 2650 kg/m³, ρf = 1000 kg/m³ and μ = 0.001 Pa·s:
v = (2650−1000)×9.81×(5×10⁻⁵)² ÷ (18×0.001) = 2.25×10⁻³ m/s = 2.25 mm/s.
Check the Reynolds number; Stokes law applies only while it is small.

keyPoints: Particle size is reported as an equivalent diameter, and the d50 is the median size of the distribution.
Screen efficiency falls when particles are close to the aperture size or the bed is too thick.
Comminution energy laws use material-specific constants that must be measured, not assumed.
At minimum fluidisation, the bed pressure drop is ΔP = (1−ε)(ρs−ρf)gL.
Stokes law gives v = (ρp−ρf)g d² ÷ (18μ) for dilute spherical particles at low Reynolds number.
Filtration rate falls as cake resistance grows; solids conveying depends on material properties and distance.

en.title: Materials and corrosion in chemical plant
en.short: Plant materials, selection, corrosion forms and prevention by design, coatings, inhibitors and cathodic protection.

sections.heading: Material families
sections.text: Metals are strong and conduct heat, so they dominate vessels and pipes. Carbon steel is cheap but rusts; stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a passive oxide film. Polymers are light and resist many acids but soften when hot. Ceramics resist heat and wear but are brittle. Composites combine fibres and a matrix for high strength at low weight. Each family has limits: a material that resists one chemical may fail in another, and temperature changes the picture.

sections.heading: Selection
sections.text: Materials selection balances duty, cost, fabrication and safety. List the chemicals, concentrations, temperatures and stresses the part will meet. Check corrosion data and compatibility tables, then compare candidates by strength, weldability and price. Design codes and standards differ between countries, so use the code that governs the plant; in Nigeria, professional registration is through COREN. A Lagos plant storing dilute sulphuric acid might choose a lined steel tank or a suitable polymer rather than plain carbon steel. Confirm the choice with the supplier and the relevant code.

sections.heading: Corrosion forms
sections.text: Corrosion is the degradation of a material by reaction with its environment. Main forms include uniform attack over the whole surface; galvanic corrosion, where two metals touch in an electrolyte and the less noble one dissolves; pitting, localised deep holes; crevice corrosion in stagnant gaps; stress corrosion cracking under tensile stress; and erosion corrosion from flowing fluid or particles. A coupon test gives rate in mm/year = 87.6 × W ÷ (D × A × t), with W in mg, D in g/cm³, A in cm² and t in hours. Example: W = 500 mg, D = 7.85, A = 20, t = 720 gives 0.39 mm/year.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Prevention starts in design: drain lines, avoid crevices, separate dissimilar metals and allow cleaning. Coatings form a barrier; inhibitors reduce attack in recirculating systems; cathodic protection makes the metal the cathode using a sacrificial anode or impressed current.

keyPoints: Metals, polymers, ceramics and composites trade strength, heat resistance, chemical resistance and cost.
Materials selection needs the full duty: chemicals, concentration, temperature, stress, fabrication and local code.
Main corrosion forms include uniform, galvanic, pitting, crevice, stress corrosion cracking and erosion corrosion.
Corrosion rate from coupon mass loss: mm/year = 87.6 × W ÷ (D × A × t), with W in mg, D in g/cm³, A in cm² and t in hours.
Prevention by design, coatings, inhibitors and cathodic protection reduces attack.
Design codes and professional registration differ by country; check the governing code and body, such as COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Process safety and loss prevention
en.short: Flammable, toxic and reactive hazards, inherent safety, HAZOP, relief, fire and explosion, and risk assessment.

sections.heading: Hazards and inherent safety
sections.text:
Flammable liquids and gases burn only within a flammable range between a lower and upper flammable limit; flash point and autoignition temperature describe ignition behaviour. Toxic materials harm by inhalation, skin contact or ingestion; exposure limits differ by country and must be checked. Reactive materials can decompose, polymerise or react violently with air, water or each other, causing runaway reactions.

Inherent safety removes or reduces a hazard at source rather than controlling it. The principles are minimise (less inventory), substitute (safer material), moderate (lower temperature or pressure) and simplify (fewer complex steps).

sections.heading: Hazard identification and HAZOP
sections.text: Hazard identification asks what can go wrong, starting early in design. Methods include checklists, what-if analysis, failure mode and effects analysis, and HAZOP (hazard and operability study). A HAZOP team divides the plant into nodes, applies guide words such as no, more, less, reverse and as well as to process parameters, and records causes, consequences and safeguards. It is structured but depends on team knowledge.

sections.heading: Relief, fire and explosion
sections.text:
Relief systems protect equipment from overpressure. A pressure relief valve opens at a set pressure; a rupture disc bursts and cannot be reseated. Relief may go to a flare or scrubber, and backpressure and two-phase flow must be considered. Relief is a last line of defence, not a substitute for control.

Fire needs fuel, oxygen and ignition. Explosions include vapour cloud explosions, dust explosions and boiling liquid expanding vapour explosions (BLEVE). Inerting and ventilation prevent flammable mixtures from forming; grounding and hazardous area classification reduce ignition sources.

sections.heading: Risk assessment
sections.text: Risk assessment estimates likelihood and consequence, then compares the result with a criterion. A simple measure is risk = frequency × consequence. Example: a leak has frequency 0.05 per year and consequence 2 serious injuries, so risk = 0.05 × 2 = 0.1 serious injuries per year. If a design change lowers frequency to 0.01 per year, risk becomes 0.02 per year. Criteria, codes and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria COREN regulates engineering practice. Check current official sources.

keyPoints: Flammable materials burn only between the lower and upper flammable limits.
Inherent safety means minimise, substitute, moderate and simplify.
HAZOP applies guide words to plant nodes to find deviations, causes and consequences.
Relief systems are a last line of defence against overpressure, not a substitute for control.
Risk can be estimated as frequency × consequence, but acceptance criteria vary by country.
Check current official codes and registration rules; in Nigeria COREN regulates engineering practice.

en.title: Process design and economics
en.short: Flowsheet synthesis, unit selection, cost estimation, profitability and sensitivity with safety.

sections.heading: Flowsheet and units
sections.text:
A flowsheet is a block or stream diagram of a process. Synthesis means choosing the reaction route, separations, recycles, heat recovery and waste handling. Unit operations are selected by duty: distillation for liquids with sufficiently different boiling points, absorption for soluble gases, filtration for solids.

Compare complete flowsheets, because one change alters recycles and utilities. Design codes, standards and professional registration differ by country, for example COREN registration in Nigeria; check the current national code.

sections.heading: Cost estimation
sections.text:
Capital cost is the money to build: equipment, installation, piping, buildings, utilities and contingency. Factorial methods multiply delivered equipment cost by empirical factors for these items; the factors vary with plant type and must come from current data.

Operating cost is annual: raw materials, utilities, labour, maintenance, overheads and waste treatment. State the estimate date and accuracy, because prices change.

sections.heading: Profitability
sections.text:
Payback period is the time to recover capital from net cash flow; it ignores later cash and the time value of money. Net present value (NPV) discounts each annual net cash flow CFt at rate r: NPV = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − capital. A positive NPV means the project earns more than r. Internal rate of return (IRR) is the r that makes NPV zero.

Example: capital £2,000,000, net cash flow £600,000 each year for 5 years, r = 10%. Annuity factor = (1 − 1.1^−5) ÷ 0.1 = 3.79079. NPV = 600,000 × 3.79079 − 2,000,000 ≈ £274,474. Payback = 2,000,000 ÷ 600,000 = 3.33 years.

sections.heading: Sensitivity and safety
sections.text:
Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time, such as product price, raw material cost, capacity or capital, and records the effect on NPV. A tornado chart ranks inputs by swing. Safety enters the same comparison: an inherently safer design may cost more but reduce expected losses.

Compare options on both risk and economics, using the codes of the country where the plant will operate.

keyPoints: NPV = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − capital; a positive NPV means the project earns more than the discount rate.
IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero.
Payback = capital ÷ annual net cash flow when the cash flow is constant.
Capital cost estimates use current factorial factors on delivered equipment cost; the factors vary with plant type.
Operating cost includes raw materials, utilities, labour, maintenance, overheads and waste treatment.
Compare flowsheet options on both safety and economics, and use the design codes of the plant’s country.

en.title: Process modelling, simulation and optimisation
en.short: Unit and flowsheet models, numerical solution, simulators and basic optimisation.

sections.heading: Models and flowsheets
sections.text:
A process model is a set of equations linking unit or flowsheet inputs to outputs. A unit model describes one item, such as a reactor. A flowsheet model connects units with streams and recycles. Steady-state models are algebraic. Dynamic models add time derivatives and often form differential-algebraic equations (DAEs). Degrees of freedom are variables minus independent equations; for a fixed design they must be zero.

Example: a constant-density CSTR with first-order reaction A → B. The steady balance Q C_A0 − Q C_A − k V C_A = 0 gives C_A = C_A0 ÷ (1 + kV/Q). With C_A0 = 2 mol/L, Q = 10 L/s, V = 100 L and k = 0.05 s⁻¹, kV/Q = 0.5, so C_A = 2 ÷ 1.5 = 1.333 mol/L. Conversion is 33.3%.

sections.heading: Solving equations
sections.text: Algebraic models are solved iteratively. Newton-Raphson linearises the equations with the Jacobian matrix and updates the unknowns until residuals are small. Linear systems use Gaussian elimination. Dynamic DAEs need numerical integration. Process simulators solve flowsheets in two main ways. Sequential modular simulators solve each unit in turn and converge recycles. Equation-oriented simulators assemble all equations and solve them together. The property package must match the chemistry and conditions.

sections.heading: Simulation in practice
sections.text: Simulation supports design, operation and improvement. It can size equipment, test a recycle, find a bottleneck or compare operating cases before plant changes. Results are only as good as the model. Check units, specifications, property data and convergence, then validate against measured plant data. Design codes and registration differ by country, for example COREN in Nigeria, so check the local code and regulator.

sections.heading: Basic optimisation
sections.text: Optimisation chooses decision variables x to minimise or maximise an objective f(x) subject to constraints g(x) ≤ 0 and h(x) = 0. Linear programming applies when f and constraints are linear; nonlinear programming (NLP) applies otherwise. Solvers may find local optima, so start from several points. Optimisation can sit around a simulator, but each run must converge.

keyPoints: A process model is a set of equations; degrees of freedom = variables − independent equations, and must be zero for a fixed design.
For a constant-density CSTR with first-order reaction, C_A = C_A0 ÷ (1 + kV/Q).
Steady-state models are algebraic, dynamic models are often differential-algebraic equations, and Newton-Raphson solves nonlinear algebraic equations using the Jacobian.
Sequential modular simulators solve units in turn and converge recycles, while equation-oriented simulators solve all equations together.
Check units, property data and convergence, then validate simulator results against measured plant data.
Optimisation minimises or maximises f(x) subject to g(x) ≤ 0 and h(x) = 0; LP is linear and NLP is nonlinear.

en.title: Environmental engineering and sustainability
en.short: Waste treatment, air and water emissions, life cycle assessment, cleaner production and circular economy.

sections.heading: Waste treatment
sections.text:
Process wastes are the unwanted gas, liquid and solid streams from a plant. Treatment reduces their load before release. Wastewater treatment often uses primary sedimentation, biological treatment, chemical precipitation, activated carbon or membranes. Air emissions are controlled with cyclones, scrubbers, adsorption, or thermal and catalytic oxidation. Solid and hazardous wastes may be stabilised, incinerated with energy recovery, or landfilled. Treatment is the last line of defence; prevention comes first.

Example: 500 m³/h of air carries 2 g/m³ of solvent vapour.
Load = 500 × 2 = 1,000 g/h = 1.0 kg/h.
A scrubber removing 90% leaves 0.10 kg/h.

sections.heading: Life cycle assessment
sections.text:
Life cycle assessment (LCA) compares products or processes from raw material extraction to disposal, often called cradle to grave. It has four stages: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation. The functional unit defines what is compared, for example 1,000 kg of product or 1 kWh of electricity. The inventory lists inputs and emissions; impact assessment converts them into categories such as climate change, acidification or water use.

A simple inventory formula is load = activity rate × emission factor. LCA helps avoid shifting a problem from one stage or medium to another.

sections.heading: Cleaner production
sections.text:
Cleaner production prevents waste at source by better design, process changes, good housekeeping, material substitution and reuse. The waste hierarchy ranks options: prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, then dispose. A circular economy keeps materials in use for longer, designs out waste and regenerates natural systems. Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own. It also means staying within environmental limits such as assimilative capacity (the pollution an environment can absorb without harm) and resource availability.

Environmental rules differ by country. In Nigeria, the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) enforces many environmental regulations; other countries have their own agencies and limits. Check the current official source for permits and limits.

keyPoints: Emission load = flow rate × concentration; removal efficiency = (inlet load − outlet load) ÷ inlet load × 100%.
Water and air treatment use physical, chemical and biological steps.
LCA has four stages: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation.
The waste hierarchy is prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose.
Cleaner production prevents waste at source, and a circular economy keeps materials in use.
Environmental regulations and limits differ by country, so check the current official source.

en.title: Biochemical engineering: enzymes, microbes and bioreactors
en.short: Enzyme kinetics, microbial growth, bioreactor operation, sterilisation and downstream processing.

sections.heading: Enzyme kinetics
sections.text:
Enzymes are protein catalysts. The Michaelis-Menten model describes a single substrate: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]), where v is reaction rate, Vmax is the maximum rate and Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax. A low Km means strong binding at low substrate concentration.

Example: Vmax = 2.0 mmol L⁻¹ min⁻¹, Km = 5 mmol L⁻¹, [S] = 15 mmol L⁻¹. v = 2.0 × 15 ÷ (5 + 15) = 1.5 mmol L⁻¹ min⁻¹. At [S] much greater than Km, v approaches Vmax.

sections.heading: Growth and products
sections.text: Microbial growth in a limiting substrate is often modelled by the Monod equation, μ = μmax S ÷ (Ks + S), where μ is specific growth rate and Ks is the half-saturation constant. Biomass yield is Yx/s = ΔX ÷ ΔS. Product formation can be described by a specific rate qp, the product formed per unit biomass, and yield Yp/s = ΔP ÷ ΔS. Products may form during growth, as with ethanol, or mainly after growth, as with many antibiotics. Temperature, pH and oxygen supply strongly affect both.

sections.heading: Bioreactors and sterilisation
sections.text: Batch culture has no feed or outflow. Fed-batch adds nutrients to extend growth. In continuous culture, fresh medium enters and broth leaves at dilution rate D = F ÷ V. At steady state D = μ; if D exceeds μmax, cells wash out. Sterilisation kills organisms by thermal death kinetics. The D-value is the time at a stated temperature to reduce viable numbers tenfold.

sections.heading: Downstream processing
sections.text: Downstream processing recovers and purifies the product. Steps may include cell disruption, centrifugation or filtration, extraction, chromatography, ultrafiltration and drying. Each step loses some product, so overall yield is the product of step yields. A plant making citric acid must balance fermentation cost against purification cost and waste treatment.

keyPoints: Michaelis-Menten rate: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]).
Monod growth: μ = μmax S ÷ (Ks + S).
Biomass yield: Yx/s = ΔX ÷ ΔS; product yield: Yp/s = ΔP ÷ ΔS.
In continuous culture at steady state, D = F ÷ V = μ; washout occurs if D > μmax.
The D-value is the time at a stated temperature to reduce viable numbers tenfold.
Overall downstream yield is the product of the yields of the individual steps.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation
en.short: Ethics, safety duty, codes and standards, and how engineers are registered.

sections.heading: Ethics and duty
sections.text: Professional ethics are the standards of conduct expected of engineers. Core duties include honesty, competence, confidentiality and avoiding conflicts of interest. A conflict of interest arises when a personal interest could improperly influence professional judgement. The public interest, especially safety and health, comes before employer or client loyalty. Engineers should state the limits of their knowledge and not sign off work outside their competence.

sections.heading: Safety responsibility
sections.text: Safety responsibility means engineers must identify hazards, follow safe designs and challenge unsafe practice. They should keep records, report concerns through proper channels, and refuse to approve work they believe is unsafe. Raising such concerns is called whistleblowing. A case: a plant engineer in Lagos finds a pressure vessel has been run above its design pressure. She reports it in writing and will not certify it as fit for service until a competent assessment is made.

sections.heading: Codes and standards
sections.text: Codes and standards are agreed technical rules. A standard is a published specification or method; a code is a broader set of design or practice rules. They are not automatically law. A standard becomes legally binding when a regulation or contract adopts it. Engineers must know which edition applies and check current national rules. In Nigeria, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) publishes national standards; other countries have their own bodies.

sections.heading: Registration and regulation
sections.text: Registration and regulation differ by country. In Nigeria, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) regulates engineering and registers engineers; the Nigerian Society of Engineers is a professional body. In the United Kingdom, the Engineering Council regulates the profession and authorises institutions such as IChemE to assess Chartered Engineer candidates. In the United States, licensure is by state boards, while AIChE is a professional society. Titles, fees and renewal rules change, so check your country’s current official source.

keyPoints: Public safety and health come before loyalty to an employer or client.
Engineers must work within their competence and must not certify work they cannot justify.
Codes and standards are technical rules; they bind legally only when adopted by regulation or contract.
Registration and regulation differ by country, so check the current official rules for your country.
In Nigeria COREN regulates engineering, while IChemE and AIChE are professional bodies in the United Kingdom and the United States respectively.
Report unsafe conditions through proper channels and keep written records.

en.title: Plant design project: capstone process design
en.short: Capstone group design: flowsheets, equipment sizing, economics, safety review and report.

sections.heading: The design brief
sections.text: A plant design project is a capstone: a group takes a product and capacity, then designs a safe, economic process. The brief fixes feed, product purity, capacity, site and constraints. It is not a single correct answer; the team compares options and records why one is chosen. Design codes and standards differ by country. In Nigeria, professional registration is through COREN, but the project should cite the current edition of each code it uses and avoid copying limits from memory.

sections.heading: Flowsheet and equipment
sections.text: The team develops a block flow diagram, then a process flow diagram (PFD) showing major equipment, streams and key conditions. Material and energy balances set stream sizes. Equipment sizing chooses type and duty, for example a heat exchanger area from Q = U A ΔT, then checks pressure drop, materials and turndown. A simulation can test the flowsheet, but the team must verify it against hand balances. Safety review starts early: identify hazards, choose inherently safer conditions, and plan relief and isolation.

sections.heading: Economics and safety
sections.text: Economic evaluation estimates fixed capital and annual operating cost, then cash flow. Payback = fixed capital ÷ annual net cash flow. For an illustrative case, fixed capital is $8,000,000 and net cash flow is $2,000,000 per year, so payback is 4 years. This ignores time value; net present value (NPV) discounts future cash flows. A hazard and operability study (HAZOP) is a structured team review of deviations such as no flow, higher pressure or wrong temperature. Findings feed the design, not just the report.

sections.heading: Report and defence
sections.text: The written report states the brief, options, selected flowsheet, balances, equipment list, cost estimate, safety review and environmental notes. It includes drawings, calculations and references. A good report lets another engineer repeat the design. The group defends the work in a presentation and answers questions on assumptions and code compliance. Keep a decision log from week one.

keyPoints: A plant design project is a group capstone that turns a brief into a safe, economic process.
The flowsheet moves from block diagram to PFD, supported by material and energy balances.
Equipment sizing uses duty equations such as Q = U A ΔT and checks pressure drop, materials and turndown.
Payback = fixed capital ÷ annual net cash flow; NPV discounts future cash flows and is preferred for long projects.
HAZOP is a structured review of process deviations and must feed design changes.
Design codes and professional registration are country-specific; in Nigeria, registration is through COREN, so cite current codes.

en.title: Advanced transport phenomena
en.short: Unified transport equations, boundary layers, turbulence, multiphase flow and CFD methods.

sections.heading: Unified equations
sections.text: All three transport processes share one conservation form. For a quantity per unit volume φ, the general equation is ∂(ρφ)/∂t + ∇·(ρuφ) = ∇·(Γ∇φ) + S. Here ρ is density, u is velocity, Γ is diffusivity and S is a source. Momentum uses velocity and viscosity; heat uses temperature and thermal conductivity; mass uses mass fraction and diffusivity. They differ mainly in source and diffusivity.

sections.heading: Boundary layers and groups
sections.text:
Near a solid surface, gradients are steep in a thin boundary layer. For laminar flow over a flat plate, the layer grows like δ ∼ √(νx/U). Heat and mass boundary layers are thinner when Prandtl number Pr = μcp/k or Schmidt number Sc = μ/(ρD) is large. Dimensionless groups link transport: Reynolds Re = ρUL/μ, Nusselt Nu = hL/k and Sherwood Sh = kcL/D. Transport analogies relate Nu, Sh and friction factor when Pr and Sc are near unity.

Example: water with ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.001 Pa·s, U = 0.5 m/s and L = 0.2 m gives Re = 1000 × 0.5 × 0.2 ÷ 0.001 = 100,000. With cp = 4180 J/(kg·K) and k = 0.6 W/(m·K), Pr = 0.001 × 4180 ÷ 0.6 = 6.97.
