sections.heading: Turbulence and multiphase
sections.text: Turbulence is chaotic, three-dimensional and diffusive. Reynolds averaging splits velocity into mean and fluctuating parts, adding Reynolds stresses that must be modelled. Eddy-viscosity models such as k-ε and k-ω are common; large-eddy simulation resolves large eddies and models small ones. Multiphase flow needs a phase description: Euler-Euler treats each phase as interpenetrating continua, while Euler-Lagrange tracks particles or bubbles. Closures for drag, lift, coalescence and turbulence modulation matter.

sections.heading: Numerical solution
sections.text: Transport equations are solved by discretising the domain and equations. The finite volume method integrates over control volumes and enforces conservation. Convection needs schemes such as upwind or limited higher-order schemes; pressure and velocity are coupled by algorithms such as SIMPLE. Stability depends on mesh quality, Courant number and turbulence model. Validation against experiment or theory is essential.

keyPoints: The general scalar transport equation is ∂(ρφ)/∂t + ∇·(ρuφ) = ∇·(Γ∇φ) + S.
Momentum, heat and mass transfer use the same conservation form with different φ, Γ and source terms.
Laminar boundary-layer thickness grows as δ ∼ √(νx/U), while Pr = μcp/k and Sc = μ/(ρD) compare diffusion rates.
Re = ρUL/μ, Nu = hL/k and Sh = kcL/D link flow, heat and mass transport.
Turbulence models close Reynolds stresses, and multiphase models use Euler-Euler or Euler-Lagrange descriptions.
Finite volume CFD enforces conservation but needs good meshes, bounded schemes and validation.

en.title: Advanced reaction engineering and catalysis
en.short: Heterogeneous catalysis, pore transport, reactor models, deactivation and advanced kinetics.

sections.heading: Heterogeneous catalysis
sections.text:
Heterogeneous catalysis uses a solid catalyst and fluid reactants. The steps are external diffusion to the pellet, pore diffusion, adsorption, surface reaction and desorption.

Intrinsic kinetics is free of transport resistance; apparent kinetics includes it. Langmuir adsorption gives rate laws such as r = kKp ÷ (1 + Kp).

sections.heading: Pore transport
sections.text:
The Thiele modulus φ = L√(k ÷ D) compares reaction with pore diffusion for a first-order slab; L is half-thickness, k the first-order rate constant (s^-1, based on pellet volume), D effective diffusivity. The effectiveness factor η is actual rate ÷ rate without pore resistance; for a slab η = tanh φ ÷ φ.

Example: L = 1 mm, k = 0.04 s^-1, D = 1 × 10^-8 m²/s. φ = 0.001√(0.04 ÷ 1 × 10^-8) = 2.0; η = tanh 2 ÷ 2 = 0.482. η near 1 means little pore resistance; η much below 1 means diffusion limitation.

sections.heading: Reactor modelling
sections.text:
Reactor models combine kinetics with flow and transport. Ideal models are batch, continuous stirred tank (CSTR) and plug flow (PFR). For a PFR at steady state, V ÷ F_A0 = ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A), where V is volume, F_A0 the feed rate of limiting reactant and X conversion.

A CSTR uses V ÷ F_A0 = X ÷ (−r_A) at outlet conditions. Real fixed beds add pressure drop, film resistance and intraparticle diffusion; the Weisz-Prater criterion, a dimensionless number comparing the measured rate with the pore diffusion rate, tests pore limitation. Multiphase reactors need a balance for each phase.

sections.heading: Deactivation and kinetics
sections.text:
Catalyst deactivation lowers activity with time. Causes include coking, sintering, poisoning and leaching. Activity a = rate at time t ÷ rate on fresh catalyst. First-order decay gives a = exp(−k_d t).

Advanced kinetic analysis fits rate laws to measured rates, checks mass and heat balances, and separates intrinsic kinetics from transport by varying pellet size, flow rate and temperature. Report confidence intervals; more parameters do not automatically mean a better model.

keyPoints: Heterogeneous catalytic rates are apparent unless pore and film transport resistances are removed or corrected.
For a first-order slab, φ = L√(k ÷ D) and η = tanh φ ÷ φ.
A steady PFR follows V ÷ F_A0 = ∫ dX ÷ (−r_A); a CSTR uses V ÷ F_A0 = X ÷ (−r_A) at outlet conditions.
Catalyst activity a = rate at time t ÷ rate on fresh catalyst; first-order decay gives a = exp(−k_d t).
The Weisz-Prater criterion is used to test whether intraparticle diffusion limits a measured rate.
Advanced kinetic analysis separates intrinsic kinetics from transport and reports parameter confidence intervals.

en.title: Process systems engineering and optimisation
en.short: Plant-wide synthesis, optimisation, scheduling, supply chains and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Systems view
sections.text: Process systems engineering treats a chemical plant as one integrated system: raw materials, reactors, separation, recycle, utilities and product specifications interact. A local change, such as extra reflux in a distillation column, alters energy use, capacity and emissions elsewhere. The aim is a plant-wide optimum, not a set of unit-wise optima. Process integration studies how material and energy are exchanged between units.

sections.heading: Synthesis and optimisation
sections.text:
Process synthesis chooses the flowsheet structure: which units, connections and recycles. A superstructure is a network containing many possible alternatives; optimisation selects one. Mathematical optimisation writes an objective function (for example annual profit or total cost) and constraints (mass and energy balances, purity, safety, capacity). Linear programming (LP) has linear equations; nonlinear programming (NLP) has nonlinear ones; mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) also has integer decisions such as yes/no for a unit. Safety and design codes enter as constraints; they differ by country, so use the current national code and regulator (for example COREN in Nigeria).

Worked example: maximise profit 30P + 20Q subject to reactor time 2P + Q ≤ 100 and packaging P + Q ≤ 80, with P,Q ≥ 0. Vertices give (50,0): 1500; (0,80): 1600; intersection P = 20, Q = 60: 30×20 + 20×60 = 1800. The optimum is 20 t of P and 60 t of Q, profit 1800.

sections.heading: Scheduling and supply chain
sections.text: Scheduling decides when batches or campaigns run, using time as a resource. It handles changeovers, cleaning, storage limits and due dates. Supply chain analysis extends the boundary from the plant to suppliers, transport, warehouses and customers. It balances inventory, lead times and service level.

sections.heading: Uncertainty
sections.text: Decision making under uncertainty recognises that prices, demand, yields and equipment availability vary. Sensitivity analysis shows which uncertain input matters most. Stochastic programming optimises expected performance over scenarios. Robust optimisation ensures feasibility for a defined range of uncertainty, often at some cost in average performance.

keyPoints: Process systems engineering optimises the integrated plant, not isolated units.
Process synthesis chooses flowsheet structure; a superstructure lists alternatives for optimisation.
Optimisation has an objective function and constraints; LP, NLP and MINLP differ by linearity and integer variables.
Scheduling allocates equipment and time; supply chain analysis extends the system to suppliers and customers.
Stochastic programming uses scenarios; robust optimisation enforces feasibility over an uncertainty set.
In the worked LP, 30P + 20Q with 2P + Q ≤ 100 and P + Q ≤ 80 gives P = 20, Q = 60 and profit 1800.

en.title: Research methods in chemical engineering
en.short: Literature review, research questions, experimental design, data analysis, modelling, ethics, writing.

sections.heading: Questions and reading
sections.text: A literature review is a systematic search and critical synthesis of what is already known. Primary sources report original work; secondary sources review it. The aim is to find a gap, not to list papers. From the gap, state a research question that is focused, answerable and feasible with your resources; for example, does coagulant dose change residual turbidity in a named water plant? A hypothesis is a testable prediction. Define the independent variable, the dependent variable and the controls before you start.

sections.heading: Experiments and data
sections.text:
Experimental design sets the factors, levels, replicates and controls so that effects can be separated from random error. Replication repeats a run; randomisation protects against bias from order or drift. Data analysis starts with means, ranges and uncertainty. A significance test asks whether a difference is larger than chance; a confidence interval gives a range for the true value. Do not confuse statistical significance with practical importance.

Worked example: two coagulant doses, 10 and 30 mg/L, with three replicates each. Mean residual turbidity is 18 NTU at 10 mg/L and 12 NTU at 30 mg/L. Estimated effect = 12 − 18 = −6 NTU. Check the replicate spread before calling this a real effect.

sections.heading: Models and ethics
sections.text: A model is a simplified mathematical representation of a process. Simulation runs that model to predict behaviour. A model is useful only after validation against independent data; report its sensitivity to assumed parameters. Research ethics covers honesty, safety, consent, waste and authorship. Do not fabricate or select data to fit a story. Cite sources and follow your institution’s rules; ethics approval requirements differ by country and university.

sections.heading: Writing the dissertation
sections.text: A dissertation argues one case in a fixed structure: introduction, literature, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. State limitations and keep records so another worker could repeat the study. Use the referencing style your department requires.

keyPoints: A literature review synthesises sources to identify a gap, not to list papers.
A research question should be focused, answerable and feasible with your resources.
Replication and randomisation reduce error and bias in experimental design.
For a two-level factor, estimated effect = mean at high level − mean at low level.
A model must be validated against independent data before its predictions are trusted.
Record data honestly, cite all sources and obtain ethics approval where your institution requires it.
